Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.question_text: $$\text{Use a separate diagram to sketch }y=\frac{2}{x^2}\text{ and }y=\frac{5}{x^2}.$$
Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.hint: $$\text{For }y=\frac{k}{x^2}:\ x\ne0,\ \text{asymptotes }x=0,\ y=0,\ \text{symmetric about y-axis. If }k_2>k_1>0,\ \frac{k_2}{x^2}\text{ lies above }\frac{k_1}{x^2}.$$
Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}\textbf{Common features (both graphs):}\\\text{Domain: }&x\ne0\\\text{Vertical asymptote: }&x=0\\\text{Horizontal asymptote: }&y=0\\\text{Symmetry: }&y\text{-axis since }f(-x)=f(x)\\\text{Position: }&y>0\text{ (both above x-axis)}\\[6pt]\textbf{Key points to plot:}\\y=\frac{2}{x^2}:&(1,2),\ (2,\tfrac12),\ (-1,2),\ (-2,\tfrac12)\\y=\frac{5}{x^2}:&(1,5),\ (2,\tfrac54),\ (-1,5),\ (-2,\tfrac54)\\[6pt]\textbf{Relative position:}\\\frac{5}{x^2}&>\frac{2}{x^2}\ \text{for all }x\ne0\\\Rightarrow\ y=\frac{5}{x^2}&\text{ is always above }y=\frac{2}{x^2}.\\[6pt]\text{Draw two upward-opening reciprocal-squared branches in quadrants I and II approaching }x=0\text{ and }y=0,\ \text{and label each curve.}\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.question_text: $$\text{Use a separate diagram to sketch }y=\frac{3}{x^2}\text{ and }y=-\frac{3}{x^2}.$$
Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.hint: $$\text{Changing the sign reflects the graph in the x-axis. Both have asymptotes }x=0,\ y=0\text{ and are symmetric about the y-axis.}$$
Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}\textbf{Common features (both graphs):}\\\text{Domain: }&x\ne0\\\text{Vertical asymptote: }&x=0\\\text{Horizontal asymptote: }&y=0\\\text{Symmetry: }&y\text{-axis since }f(-x)=f(x)\\[6pt]\textbf{For }y=\frac{3}{x^2}:\\&k>0\Rightarrow y>0\text{ so branches are above the x-axis (quadrants I and II).}\\\text{Points: }&(1,3),\ (2,\tfrac34),\ (-1,3),\ (-2,\tfrac34)\\[6pt]\textbf{For }y=-\frac{3}{x^2}:\\&k<0\Rightarrow y<0\text{ so branches are below the x-axis (quadrants III and IV).}\\&\text{This is the reflection of }y=\frac{3}{x^2}\text{ in the x-axis.}\\\text{Points: }&(1,-3),\ (2,-\tfrac34),\ (-1,-3),\ (-2,-\tfrac34)\\[6pt]\text{Sketch both sets of branches approaching }x=0\text{ and }y=0,\ \text{and label each curve clearly.}\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.question_text: $$\text{Use a separate diagram to sketch }y=-\frac{2}{x^2}\text{ and }y=-\frac{6}{x^2}.$$
Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.hint: $$\text{Both have }k<0\Rightarrow\text{ both curves lie below the x-axis; larger }|k|\text{ gives values further down (more negative).}$$
Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}\textbf{Common features (both graphs):}\\\text{Domain: }&x\ne0\\\text{Vertical asymptote: }&x=0\\\text{Horizontal asymptote: }&y=0\\\text{Symmetry: }&y\text{-axis since }f(-x)=f(x)\\\text{Position: }&y<0\text{ (both below x-axis, in quadrants III and IV)}\\[6pt]\textbf{Key points to plot:}\\y=-\frac{2}{x^2}:&(1,-2),\ (2,-\tfrac12),\ (-1,-2),\ (-2,-\tfrac12)\\y=-\frac{6}{x^2}:&(1,-6),\ (2,-\tfrac32),\ (-1,-6),\ (-2,-\tfrac32)\\[6pt]\textbf{Relative position:}\\-\frac{6}{x^2}&<-\frac{2}{x^2}\ \text{for all }x\ne0\\\Rightarrow\ y=-\frac{6}{x^2}&\text{ lies below }y=-\frac{2}{x^2}\text{ everywhere.}\\[6pt]\text{Draw two downward reciprocal-squared branches in quadrants III and IV approaching }x=0\text{ and }y=0,\ \text{and label each curve.}\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.question_text: $$\text{(a) On the same axes sketch the curves }y=(x+1)^3\text{ and }y=3x(x-1).\ \text{(b) Explain how your sketch shows that there is only one real solution to }x^3+6x+1=0.$$
Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.hint: $$\text{At intersection points }(x+1)^3=3x(x-1).\ \text{The number of real solutions equals the number of intersections.}$$
Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}\textbf{Curve }y=(x+1)^3:&\ \text{increasing cubic for all }x\\\text{x-intercept: }(x+1)^3=0&\Rightarrow x=-1\\\text{y-intercept: }x=0&\Rightarrow y=1\\[6pt]\textbf{Curve }y=3x(x-1):&=3x^2-3x\ \text{(upward parabola)}\\\text{x-intercepts: }&x=0,\ 1\\\text{Vertex: }&x=\tfrac12,\ y=-\tfrac34\\[8pt]\textbf{Intersections:}\\(x+1)^3&=3x(x-1)\\x^3+3x^2+3x+1&=3x^2-3x\\x^3+6x+1&=0\\[6pt]\text{From the sketch, the graphs intersect once only.}\\\therefore\ \text{the equation has exactly one real solution.}\end{aligned}$$
$$f(x)=x^2-x^3,\ x^2(1-x)=0\Rightarrow x=0\text{ (double root)},1;\ y\text{-intercept }(0,0);\ \text{cubic touching x-axis at }(0,0)\text{ and crossing at }(1,0).$$
$$y=f(x+1)\text{ is the graph of }y=f(x)\text{ shifted }1\text{ unit to the left.}$$

Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.question_text: $$\text{The point }P(2,1)\text{ lies on }y=f(x).\ \text{On the graph of }y=af(x),\ P\text{ maps to }Q(4,1).\ \text{Determine }a.$$
Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.hint: $$\text{For }y=af(x),\ x\text{ stays the same and }y\text{ is multiplied by }a.$$
Chapter 4 - Graphs and transforma.correct_answer: $$\text{Under }y=af(x),\ (x,y)\mapsto(x,ay).\ \text{So }P(2,1)\mapsto(2,a).\ \text{Given image is }Q(4,1)\text{ (same y as original), this indicates a horizontal stretch by factor }2\text{, i.e. }y=f\!\left(\tfrac{x}{2}\right).\ \text{But if the intended transformation is }y=af(x)\text{ then }x\text{ cannot change, so the only consistent value is }a=1.$$

$$\text{The diagram shows the curve }y=5+2x-x^2\text{ and the line }y=2.\ \text{The curve and the line intersect at points }A\text{ and }B.\ \text{Find the x-coordinates of }A\text{ and }B.$$

(b) Find where it crosses the y-axis (A). The line $$l_2$$ passes through the origin with gradient 3. The lines intersect at B. (c) Find coordinates of B. (d) Find the exact area of $$\triangle OAB$$.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Use point–slope form $$y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$$ to get $$l_1$$, then set $$x=0$$ for A, solve simultaneously for B, then area formula $$\tfrac12|x_Ay_B-y_Ax_B|.$$
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.correct_answer: (a) $$y-14=-\tfrac14(x+4)\Rightarrow y=-\tfrac14x+13$$ → $$x+4y-52=0.$$ (b) At $$x=0,$$ $$y=13$$ → $$A(0,13).$$ (c) For $$l_2:y=3x,$$ solve $$3x=-\tfrac14x+13\Rightarrow 13=\tfrac{13x}{4}\Rightarrow x=4,\ y=12\Rightarrow B(4,12).$$ (d) $$\text{Area}=\tfrac12|0\cdot12-13\cdot4|=\tfrac12(52)=26.$$

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: A website designer charges a flat fee and a daily rate. Company A’s site takes 6 days and costs £7100; Company B’s takes 13 days and costs £9550. (a) Write an equation linking days $$d$$ and cost $$C$$ in the form $$C=ad+b$$. (b) Interpret $$a$$ and $$b$$. (c) If a third company is charged £13 400, find the number of days.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Set up two points $$(d,C)=(6,7100),(13,9550)$$ and fit $$C=ad+b$$.

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: The average August temperature in Exeter is $$20^\circ\text{C}$$ or $$68^\circ\text{F}$$; the average January temperature is $$9^\circ\text{C}$$ or $$48.2^\circ\text{F}$$. (a) Find a linear equation linking Fahrenheit $$F$$ and Celsius $$C$$ in the form $$F=aC+b$$. (b) Interpret $$a,b$$. (c) Convert the UK record of $$101.3^\circ\text{F}$$ to Celsius. (d) For what value is the temperature the same in both scales?
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Use the two points $$(C,F)=(20,68),(9,48.2)$$ to determine $$a,b$$; then invert to convert; solve $$F=C$$.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.correct_answer: (a) $$a=\dfrac{68-48.2}{20-9}=1.8=\tfrac{9}{5},\ b=68-1.8\cdot20=32\Rightarrow F=\tfrac{9}{5}C+32.$$ (b) $$a=\tfrac{9}{5}$$ is the scale factor; $$b=32$$ is the offset (freezing point). (c) $$C=\dfrac{101.3-32}{1.8}=38.5^\circ\text{C}.$$ (d) $$C=F\Rightarrow C=1.8C+32\Rightarrow C=-40,$$ so $$-40^\circ$$ on both scales.

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: In 2004 a city had 17 500 homes with internet connections. A service provider predicts an additional 750 homes will get internet each year after 2004. (a) Write a linear model for the number of homes $$n$$ with internet connections $$t$$ years after 2004. (b) State one assumption of this model.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Model linear growth from initial value.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.correct_answer: (a) $$n=17500+750t.$$ (b) Assumes the increase is constant at 750 homes per year (linear growth) and other factors remain unchanged.

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: The points $$A(2,16)$$ and $$B(12,-4)$$ have coordinates as shown. A straight line $$l_1$$ passes through $$A$$ and $$B$$. (a) Find an equation for $$l_1$$ in the form $$ax+by=c.$$ The line $$l_2$$ passes through the point $$C(-1,1)$$ and has gradient $$\tfrac{1}{3}.$$ (b) Find an equation for $$l_2.$$
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Use gradient between $$A$$ and $$B$$, apply point–slope form, and rearrange to $$ax+by=c.$$

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: The points $$A(-1,-2),\ B(7,2),\ C(k,4)$$ are the vertices of $$\triangle ABC$$, where angle $$ABC$$ is a right angle. (a) Find the gradient of $$AB$$. (b) Calculate the value of $$k$$. (c) Find an equation of the straight line passing through $$B$$ and $$C$$ in the form $$ax+by+c=0$$. (d) Calculate the area of $$\triangle ABC.$$
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Use gradient formula for perpendicular lines and right-angle condition $$m_{AB}\times m_{BC}=-1.$$
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.correct_answer: (a) $$m_{AB}=\tfrac{2-(-2)}{7-(-1)}=\tfrac{4}{8}=\tfrac{1}{2}.$$ (b) For right angle at $$B,$$ $$m_{AB}\cdot m_{BC}=-1\Rightarrow\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot m_{BC}=-1\Rightarrow m_{BC}=-2.$$ Using $$B(7,2)$$ and $$C(k,4):4-2=-2(k-7)\Rightarrow k=8.$$ (c) $$m_{BC}=-2,\ y-2=-2(x-7)\Rightarrow2x+y-16=0.$$ (d) Base $$AB=8\sqrt{1^2+(0.5)^2}=\sqrt{80}=8.94,$$ height $$=|4-2|=2,$$ so $$\text{Area}=\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot8\cdot4=16.$$

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: Find an equation of the straight line passing through the points with coordinates $$(-1,5)$$ and $$(4,-2)$$, giving your answer in the form $$ax+by+c=0$$, where $$a,b,c$$ are integers. The line crosses the x-axis at point $$A$$ and the y-axis at point $$B$$, and $$O$$ is the origin. (a) Find an equation of the line. (b) Find the area of $$\triangle AOB.$$
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Find gradient and use two-point form, then use intercepts to calculate area with coordinate formula.

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: The straight line $$l_1$$ has equation $$4y+x=0.$$ The straight line $$l_2$$ has equation $$y=2x-3.$$ (a) On the same axes, sketch both lines showing coordinates of intercepts. (b) The lines $$l_1$$ and $$l_2$$ intersect at point $$A$$. Calculate exact fractions for $$A$$. (c) Find an equation of the line through $$A$$ which is perpendicular to $$l_1$$, in the form $$ax+by+c=0.$$
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Use intercepts, substitution, and perpendicular slope relation $$m_1m_2=-1.$$
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.correct_answer: (a) For $$l_1:4y+x=0\Rightarrow y=-\tfrac{1}{4}x$$ (passes through $$(0,0)$$ and $$(4,-1)$$). For $$l_2:y=2x-3$$ (intercepts $$(0,-3)$$ and $$(\tfrac{3}{2},0)$$). (b) Intersection: $$-\tfrac{1}{4}x=2x-3\Rightarrow9x=12\Rightarrow x=\tfrac{4}{3},y=-\tfrac{1}{3}\Rightarrow A(\tfrac{4}{3},-\tfrac{1}{3}).$$ (c) $$m_{l_1}=-\tfrac{1}{4}\Rightarrow m_\perp=4.$$ Equation through $$A: y+\tfrac{1}{3}=4(x-\tfrac{4}{3})\Rightarrow4x-y-\tfrac{17}{3}=0\Rightarrow12x-3y-17=0.$$

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: The points $$A(4,6)$$ and $$B(12,2)$$ are given. The straight line $$l_1$$ passes through $$A$$ and $$B.$$ (a) Find the equation of $$l_1$$ in the form $$ax+by+c=0.$$ The straight line $$l_2$$ passes through the origin and has gradient $$-\tfrac{2}{3}.$$ (b) Write down an equation for $$l_2.$$ The lines $$l_1$$ and $$l_2$$ intersect at point $$C.$$ (c) Find the coordinates of $$C.$$ (d) Show that lines $$OA$$ and $$OC$$ are perpendicular, where $$O$$ is the origin. (e) Work out the lengths of $$OA$$ and $$OC$$ in the form $$k\sqrt{13}.$$ (f) Hence calculate the area of $$\triangle OAC.$$
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Use two-point form for $$l_1$$, solve for intersection, then apply perpendicularity and distance formula.
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.correct_answer: (a) $$m=\tfrac{2-6}{12-4}=-\tfrac{1}{2},\ y-6=-\tfrac{1}{2}(x-4)\Rightarrow x+2y-16=0.$$ (b) $$y=-\tfrac{2}{3}x.$$ (c) Solve $$x+2(-\tfrac{2}{3}x)-16=0\Rightarrow -\tfrac{1}{3}x=16\Rightarrow x=-48,\ y=32\Rightarrow C(-48,32).$$ (d) $$m_{OA}=\tfrac{6-0}{4-0}=\tfrac{3}{2},\ m_{OC}=\tfrac{32-0}{-48-0}=-\tfrac{2}{3},\ m_{OA}m_{OC}=-1\Rightarrow\text{perpendicular.}$$ (e) $$OA=\sqrt{4^2+6^2}=\sqrt{52}=2\sqrt{13},\ OC=\sqrt{(-48)^2+32^2}=\sqrt{64\times52}=8\sqrt{13}.$$ (f) $$\text{Area}=\tfrac{1}{2}(OA\times OC)=\tfrac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{13}\times8\sqrt{13})=104.$$

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: Point $$A$$ is $$(-1,5).$$ Let $$(x,y)$$ be any point on the line $$y=3x.$$ (a) Write an equation in terms of $$x$$ for the distance between $$(x,y)$$ and $$A(-1,5).$$ (b) Find coordinates of the two points $$B$$ and $$C$$ on the line $$y=3x$$ that are a distance of $$\sqrt{74}$$ from $$(-1,5).$$ (c) Find the equation of the line $$l_1$$ perpendicular to $$y=3x$$ and passing through $$(-1,5).$$ (d) Find the coordinates of the intersection of $$l_1$$ and $$y=3x.$$ (e) Find the area of $$\triangle ABC.$$
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Use distance formula, substitution, perpendicular slope relation, and area formula.

Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.question_text: Find the area of the triangle with vertices $$A(-2,-2),\ B(13,8),\ C(-4,14).$$
Chapter 5 - Straight line graphs.hint: Use coordinate area formula $$\text{Area}=\tfrac12|x_1(y_2-y_3)+x_2(y_3-y_1)+x_3(y_1-y_2)|.$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The line segment $$FG$$ is a diameter of a circle centre $$C(6,1).$$ Given $$F(2,-3),$$ find $$G.$$
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Use midpoint relation $$6=\tfrac{2+x_G}{2},1=\tfrac{-3+y_G}{2}.$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The line segment $$CD$$ is a diameter of a circle centre $$(-2a,5a).$$ Given $$D(3a,-7a),$$ find $$C.$$
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Use midpoint formula backward.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: $$(-2a,5a)=\!\left(\tfrac{C_x+3a}{2},\tfrac{C_y-7a}{2}\right)\!\Rightarrow C(-7a,17a).$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: Points $$M(3,p),N(4,q)$$ lie on a circle centre $$(5,6).$$ The diameter $$MN$$ has midpoint $$(5,6).$$ Find $$p,q.$$
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Set midpoint conditions $$\tfrac{3+4}{2}=5,\ \tfrac{p+q}{2}=6.$$
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: $$p+q=12\Rightarrow(p,q)=(4,8)\text{ or any satisfying sum 12.}$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: Point $$X(7,-2)$$ and point $$Y(4,q)$$. The perpendicular bisector of $$XY$$ has equation $$y=4x+b$$. Find the values of $$q$$ and $$b$$.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Use slope condition $$m_\perp\cdot m_{XY}=-1$$ and midpoint lies on bisector.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: From $$m_\perp=4$$, $$m_{XY}=-\tfrac14=\tfrac{q+2}{4-7}=-\tfrac{q+2}{3}\Rightarrow q=-\tfrac54.$$ Midpoint $$M(\tfrac{7+4}{2},\tfrac{-2+q}{2})=(\tfrac{11}{2},-\tfrac{13}{8}).$$ On $$y=4x+b$$: $$-\tfrac{13}{8}=4\cdot\tfrac{11}{2}+b\Rightarrow b=-\tfrac{189}{8}.$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: Triangle $$PQR$$ has vertices $$P(6,9),Q(3,-3),R(-9,3).$$ (a) Find the perpendicular bisectors of each side of the triangle. (b) Show that all three perpendicular bisectors meet at a single point and find its coordinates.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Midpoints and perpendicular slopes for $$PQ,QR,PR$$; write their equations and solve any two to get the circumcenter.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: $$\text{Bisector of }PQ:\ 2x+8y-33=0;\quad \text{of }QR:\ 2x-y+6=0;\quad \text{of }PR:\ 10x+4y-9=0.$$ Solving (first two): $$x=-\tfrac{5}{6},\ y=\tfrac{13}{3}.$$ Substituting into the third satisfies it, so all three concur at $$\big(-\tfrac{5}{6},\tfrac{13}{3}\big).$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: A circle $$C$$ has equation $$x^2+y^2+12x+2y=k,$$ where $$k$$ is constant. (a) Find centre of $$C.$$ (b) State range of possible values of $$k.$$
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Complete the square in $$x,y$$.

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The point $$P(7,-14)$$ lies on the circle $$x^2+y^2+6x-14y=17$$. The point $$Q$$ also lies on the circle such that $$PQ$$ is a diameter. Find coordinates of $$Q.$$
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Find centre via completing squares, then use midpoint condition $$\text{Mid}(P,Q)=\text{centre}$$.

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The circle with equation $$(x-k)^2+y^2=41$$ passes through $$(3,4)$$. Find two possible values of $$k.$$
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Substitute point and solve for $$k$$.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: $$(3-k)^2+4^2=41\Rightarrow(3-k)^2=25\Rightarrow3-k=\pm5\Rightarrow k=-2\text{ or }8.$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: A circle with equation $$(x-k)^2+(y-2)^2=50$$ passes through the point $$(4,-5).$$ Find the possible values of $$k$$ and the equation of each circle.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Substitute the point and solve for $$k$$; then write both circle equations.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: Hence, $$(x-k)^2+(y-2)^2=50$$ passes through the point $$(4,-5)$$. Put the value of the x, y in equation, $$(4-k)^2+(-5-2)^2=50\Rightarrow(4-k)^2+49=50\Rightarrow(4-k)^2=1.$$ Hence $$4-k=\pm1\Rightarrow k=3\ \text{or}\ k=5.$$ Therefore the two circles are $$\boxed{(x-3)^2+(y-2)^2=50}$$ and $$\boxed{(x-5)^2+(y-2)^2=50}$$ (same radius, centres at $$(3,2)$$ and $$(5,2)$$, both 1 unit horizontally from the point’s perpendicular through the centre).

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: By completing the square for $$x$$ and $$y$$, show that the equation $$x^2+y^2+2fx+2gy+c=0$$ describes a circle with centre $$(-f,-g)$$ and radius $$\sqrt{f^2+g^2-c}.$$
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Rearrange and complete the square in each variable.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: Group: $$(x^2+2fx)+(y^2+2gy)+c=0.$$ Complete squares: $$(x+f)^2-f^2+(y+g)^2-g^2+c=0\Rightarrow (x+f)^2+(y+g)^2=f^2+g^2-c.$$ Hence the centre is $$(-f,-g)$$ and $$r^2=f^2+g^2-c$$ (so a real circle requires $$f^2+g^2-c>0$$).

Chapter 6 - Circles.subtopic_name: Intersections of straight lines and circles
Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The circle with equation $$(x-4)^2+(y+7)^2=50$$ meets the line $$x-y-5=0$$ at $$A,B$$. (a) Find the coordinates of of the points $$A,B$$. (b) Find the equation perpendicular bisector of line segment $$AB$$. (c) Show this bisector of AB passes through the circle’s centre. (d) Find the area of $$\triangle OAB$$.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Use $$y=x-5$$ in the circle; midpoint–slope for bisector; check centre; area with base–height.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: (a) Substitute: $$(x-4)^2+(x+2)^2=50\Rightarrow2x^2-4x-30=0\Rightarrow x=5,-3.$$ Then $$y=x-5\Rightarrow A(5,0),\ B(-3,-8).$$ (b) $$M=\big(\tfrac{5+(-3)}{2},\tfrac{0+(-8)}{2}\big)=(1,-4),\ m_{AB}=1\Rightarrow m_\perp=-1,$$ so $$y+4=-1(x-1)\Rightarrow x+y+3=0.$$ (c) Centre $$C(4,-7):\ 4+(-7)+3=0\Rightarrow C$$ lies on the bisector. (d) Base $$OA=5$$ on the $$x$$-axis, height $$=|y_B|=8,$$ so $$\text{Area}=\tfrac12\cdot5\cdot8=\boxed{20}.$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.subtopic_name: Intersections of straight lines and circles
Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The line $$y=kx$$ intersects the circle $$x^2-10x+y^2-12y+57=0$$ at two distinct points. (a) Show that $$21k^2-60k+32<0.$$ (b) Hence find the range of the possible value of  $$k$$.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Substitute $$y=kx$$ and require discriminant $$>0$$.

Chapter 6 - Circles.subtopic_name: Intersections of straight lines and circles
Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The line $$y=4x-1$$ does not intersect the circle $$x^2+2x+y^2=k$$. Find the range of possible values of $$k$$.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Substitute and set discriminant $$<0$$; also require a real circle.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: $$x^2+2x+(4x-1)^2=k\Rightarrow 17x^2-6x+1-k=0.$$ $$\Delta=(-6)^2-4\cdot17(1-k)<0\Rightarrow36-68(1-k)<0\Rightarrow k<\tfrac{8}{17}.$$ Since a circle needs $$k>-1$$ (because $$(x+1)^2+y^2=k+1$$), range $$\boxed{-1<k<\tfrac{8}{17}}.$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.subtopic_name: Intersections of straight lines and circles
Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The line $$y=2x+5$$ meets the circle $$x^2+kx+y^2=4$$ at exactly one point. Find the two possible values of $$k$$.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Substitute and set discriminant $$=0$$.

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The Circle has the equation $$ x^2+18x+y^2-2y+29=0.$$ (a) Verify $$P(-7,-6)$$ lies on $$C$$. (b) Find an equation of the tangent to $$C$$ at $$P$$ in the form $$y=mx+b$$. (c) Find the coordinates of $$R,$$ the intersection of this tangent with the $$y$$-axis. (d) Find the area of $$\triangle APR,$$ where $$A$$ is the centre of $$C$$.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Complete squares for centre; use radius–tangent perpendicularity; for (d) use area $$\tfrac12|x_A(y_P-y_R)+x_P(y_R-y_A)+x_R(y_A-y_P)|$$ or vector determinant.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: (a) $$49-126+36+12+29=0\Rightarrow P\in C.$$ (b) $$(x+9)^2+(y-1)^2=53\Rightarrow A(-9,1).$$ Radius slope $$=\tfrac{-6-1}{-7-(-9)}=-\tfrac72\Rightarrow m_t=\tfrac{2}{7}.$$ Tangent: $$y+6=\tfrac{2}{7}(x+7)\Rightarrow \boxed{y=\tfrac{2}{7}x-4}.$$ (c) Set $$x=0\Rightarrow R(0,-4).$$ (d) $$A(-9,1),P(-7,-6),R(0,-4).$$ Area $$=\tfrac12|\,\det(\overrightarrow{AP},\overrightarrow{AR})\,|=\tfrac12|\,\langle2,-7\rangle\times\langle9,-5\rangle\,|=\tfrac12|(-10+63)|=\boxed{\tfrac{53}{2}}.$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The tangent to the circle $$(x+4)^2+(y-1)^2=242$$ at $$(7,-10)$$ meets the $$y$$-axis at $$S$$ and the $$x$$-axis at $$T$$. (a) Find $$S,T$$. (b) Hence find the area of $$\triangle OST$$ where $$O$$ is the origin.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Find tangent eqn using point–radius perpendicularity, then find intercepts.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: (a) Centre $$(-4,1)$$; radius slope $$=\tfrac{-10-1}{7+4}=-1.$$ Hence tangent slope $$=1$$. Through $$(7,-10): y+10=1(x-7)\Rightarrow y=x-17.$$ For $$S$$: $$x=0\Rightarrow y=-17\Rightarrow S(0,-17);$$ for $$T$$: $$y=0\Rightarrow x=17\Rightarrow T(17,0).$$ (b) Area $$=\tfrac12|x_Ty_S-x_Sy_T|=\tfrac12(17\times17)=\boxed{144.5}.$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The circle $$C$$ has centre $$P(11,-5)$$ and passes through $$Q(5,3)$$. (a) Find the equation of $$C$$. (b) The line $$l_1$$ is tangent to $$C$$ at $$Q$$ — find its equation. (c) The line $$l_2$$ is parallel to $$l_1$$ and passes through the midpoint of $$PQ$$; it meets $$C$$ at $$A,B$$. Find the coordinates of $$A,B$$. (d) Find the length $$AB$$ in simplest surd form.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Use distance formula for radius; tangent ⟂ radius; parallel line through midpoint; intersection via substitution; distance formula for $$AB$$.

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_title: Circle from two points (line through centre)
Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The points $$R(2,3)$$ and $$S(10,1)$$ lie on a circle with centre $$C(a,-2)$$. Let $$M$$ be the midpoint of $$RS$$. The line $$l$$ passes through $$M$$ and $$C$$. (a) Find an equation of $$l$$. (b) Find the value of $$a$$. (c) Find the equation of the circle. (d) Find the points of intersection, $$A$$ and $$B$$, of the line $$l$$ and the circle.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Use midpoint for $$M$$; slope of $$MC$$ for $$l$$; set $$CR=CS$$ to get $$a$$; circle $$(x-a)^2+(y+2)^2=r^2$$ with $$r^2=CR^2$$; substitute $$l$$ into circle for $$A,B$$.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: (a) $$M(6,2),\ C(a,-2)\Rightarrow m=\dfrac{-2-2}{a-6}=\dfrac{-4}{a-6};\ \text{with }a=5\Rightarrow m=4,\ l:\ y-2=4(x-6)\iff y=4x-22.$$ (b) $$CR^2=CS^2\Rightarrow(2-a)^2+5^2=(10-a)^2+3^2\Rightarrow a=5.$$ (c) $$r^2=(2-5)^2+(3+2)^2=34\Rightarrow (x-5)^2+(y+2)^2=34.$$ (d) Solve $$y=4x-22$$ with circle: $$x=5\pm\sqrt2,\ y=-2\pm4\sqrt2;$$ so $$A\!\left(5+\sqrt2,\,-2+4\sqrt2\right),\ B\!\left(5-\sqrt2,\,-2-4\sqrt2\right).$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The points $$A(-1,9),~B(6,10),~C(7,3),~D(0,2)$$ lie on a circle. (a) Show $$ABCD$$ is a square. (b) Find its area. (c) Find the centre of the circle.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Show sides equal and perpendicular using vectors; centre is midpoint of diagonal.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: (a) $$\overrightarrow{AB}=(7,1),~\overrightarrow{BC}=(1,-7),$$ with $$|\overrightarrow{AB}|^2=|\overrightarrow{BC}|^2=50,$$ and $$\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=7(1)+1(-7)=0$$ ⇒ sides equal and perpendicular ⇒ square. (b) Area $$=\text{side}^2=50.$$ (c) Centre = midpoint of diagonal $$A,C$$: $$\Big(\frac{-1+7}{2},\frac{9+3}{2}\Big)=(3,6).$$ Radius $$r=\sqrt{50}/2=5.$$ Hence circle $$\boxed{(x-3)^2+(y-6)^2=25}. $$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The points $$D(-12,-3),~E(-10,b),~F(2,-5)$$ lie on a circle with $$\angle DEF=90^\circ$$ and $$b>0$$. (a) Find $$b$$. (b) Find the equation of the circle.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: For perpendicular lines: $$m_{DE}\cdot m_{EF}=-1$$; a right angle subtends a diameter ⇒ centre is midpoint of diameter $$DF$$.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: (a) $$m_{DE}=\frac{b+3}{2},~m_{EF}=\frac{-5-b}{12},~m_{DE}m_{EF}=-1\Rightarrow-\frac{(b+3)(b+5)}{24}=-1\Rightarrow b^2+8b-9=0.$$ So $$b=\frac{-8\pm\sqrt{100}}{2}=1,-9$$ and since $$b>0\Rightarrow\boxed{b=1}.$$ (b) Right angle at $$E$$ ⇒ diameter is $$DF$$. Centre $$O=\Big(\frac{-12+2}{2},\frac{-3+(-5)}{2}\Big)=(-5,-4).$$ Radius squared $$r^2=OD^2=(7)^2+(-1)^2=50.$$ Hence $$\boxed{(x+5)^2+(y+4)^2=50}.$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The circle has equation $$x^2+2x+y^2-24y-24=0.$$ (a) Find the centre and radius of the circle. (b) The points $$A(-13,17)$$ and $$B(11,7)$$ lie on the circumference. Show that $$AB$$ is a diameter. (c) The point $$C$$ lies on the negative x-axis and the angle $$ACB=90^\circ$$. Find the coordinates of $$C$$.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Complete the square to find the centre and radius; check that A,B satisfy the circle and midpoint equals centre. Use circle geometry (right angle in semicircle).
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: (a) Rewrite: $$(x^2+2x+1)+(y^2-24y+144)=24+1+144\Rightarrow(x+1)^2+(y-12)^2=169.$$ Hence centre $$(-1,12)$$ and radius $$13$$. (b) Midpoint of $$A,B$$ is $$\Big(\frac{-13+11}{2},\frac{17+7}{2}\Big)=(-1,12),$$ equal to centre ⇒ $$AB$$ is a diameter. (c) Right angle on semicircle ⇒ $$C$$ lies on circle and $$\angle ACB=90^\circ$$ ⇒ x-axis (y=0). Substitute $$y=0$$ in circle: $$(x+1)^2+(0-12)^2=169\Rightarrow x^2+2x+1+144=169\Rightarrow x^2+2x-24=0\Rightarrow(x+6)(x-4)=0,$$ so $$x=-6$$ or $$x=4$$. Negative x-axis ⇒ $$\boxed{C(-6,0)}.$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The circle $$C$$ has equation $$(x-3)^2+(y+3)^2=52.$$ The baselines $$l_1$$ and $$l_2$$ are tangents to the circle and have gradient $$\frac{4}{3}$$. (a) Find the points of intersection $$P,Q$$ of the tangents and the circle. (b) Find the equations of $$l_1$$ and $$l_2$$, giving your answers in the form $$ax+by+c=0.$$
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Use line form $$y=mx+c$$, substitute in circle, and use discriminant $$=0$$ to find possible $$c$$ values (tangent condition).

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The circle $$C$$ has equation $$x^2+6x+y^2-2y=7.$$ The lines $$l_1$$ and $$l_2$$ are tangents to the circle meeting at the point $$(10,6).$$ Find (a) the equations of $$l_1$$ and $$l_2$$, (b) the points of intersection $$P,Q$$ of the tangents with the circle, (c) the area of quadrilateral $$APRQ$$.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Find circle’s centre and radius by completing square, use tangent condition (discriminant = 0) to find slopes.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: (a) Complete the square: $$(x+3)^2+(y-1)^2=17,$$ centre $(-3,1)$, radius $\sqrt{17}$. Tangent form $y-6=m(x-10)$, substitute in circle, discriminant = 0: $$(x+3)^2+[m(x-10)+5]^2=17.$$ Expand and solve ⇒ quadratic in $x$: $$(1+m^2)x^2+2x[3+m(5-10m)] +[...] = 0.$$ Discriminant $=0$ ⇒ $$m^2+10m-3=0$$ ⇒ $$m_1=-5+2\sqrt{7},~m_2=-5-2\sqrt{7}.$$ (b) Substitute each $m$ into line equation to find $P,Q$. (c) Use coordinate geometry area formula for quadrilateral.

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The circle $$C$$ has centre $$(6,9)$$ and radius $$\sqrt{50}.$$ The line $$l$$ with equation $$x+y-21=0$$ intersects the circle at the points $$P,Q$$. (a) Find the coordinates of $$P$$ and $$Q$$. (b) Find equations of the tangents $$l_1$$ and $$l_2$$ at $$P,Q$$ respectively. (c) Find the equation of the line perpendicular bisector of chord $$PQ$$. (d) Show that the two tangents and the perpendicular bisector intersect at one point $$R$$, and find $$R$$. (e) Calculate the area of the kite $$APRQ$$.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Substitute $$y=21-x$$ into circle and solve; find tangent slopes from radii, then bisector and intersection.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: (a) Sub: $$(x-6)^2+(21-x-9)^2=50\Rightarrow(x-6)^2+(12-x)^2=50\Rightarrow2x^2-36x+180=50\Rightarrow2x^2-36x+130=0\Rightarrow x^2-18x+65=0.$$ Roots $$x=13,5$$ ⇒ $$P(13,8),~Q(5,16).$$ (b) Radii slopes: $$m_P=\frac{8-9}{13-6}=-\frac{1}{7}\Rightarrow m_{t1}=7,$$ $$m_Q=\frac{16-9}{5-6}=-7\Rightarrow m_{t2}=\frac{1}{7}.$$ Tangents: $$l_1: y-8=7(x-13)\Rightarrow7x-y-83=0,$$ $$l_2: y-16=\frac{1}{7}(x-5)\Rightarrow x-7y+107=0.$$ (c) Midpoint of $$PQ(9,12)$$, slope $$m_{PQ}=\frac{16-8}{5-13}=-1\Rightarrow m_\perp=1$$ ⇒ $$y-12=x-9\Rightarrow x-y+3=0.$$ (d) Solve $$7x-y-83=0,~x-y+3=0$$ ⇒ $$x=12.57,~y=15.57$$ ⇒ $$R(12.57,15.57).$$ All three intersect at $$R$$. (e) Use kite area formula with diagonals.

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The line $$y=-3x+12$$ meets the coordinate axes at $$A$$ and $$B$$. The line segment $$AB$$ is a diameter of a circle. Find the equation of the circle.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Find intercepts, midpoint, and radius from half the diagonal.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: Intercepts: at x-axis (y=0): $$x=4\Rightarrow A(4,0)$$; at y-axis (x=0): $$y=12\Rightarrow B(0,12).$$ Centre = midpoint $$O(2,6),$$ radius $$r^2=(4-2)^2+(0-6)^2=4+36=40.$$ Equation: $$\boxed{(x-2)^2+(y-6)^2=40.}$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The points $$A(-3,-2),~B(-6,0),~C(1,9)$$ lie on the circumference of a circle such that $$\angle ABC=90^\circ.$$ (a) Find the value of $$q$$. (b) Find the equation of the circle.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Use right-angle property ⇒ $$AC$$ is diameter, then midpoint gives centre and distance gives radius.

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The points $$R(-4,3),~S(7,4),~T(8,-7)$$ lie on the circumference of a circle. (a) Show that $$RT$$ is the diameter of the circle. (b) Find the equation of the circle.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Check $$RS^2+ST^2=RT^2$$ or midpoint of RT equals circle’s centre.

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The points $$A(-4,0),~B(4,8),~C(6,0)$$ lie on the circumference of a circle. Find the equation of the circle.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Use perpendicular bisectors of two chords.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: Chord $$AB:~M_{AB}(0,4),~m_{AB}=\frac{8-0}{4-(-4)}=1\Rightarrow m_\perp=-1.$$ ⇒ $$y-4=-1(x-0)\Rightarrow x+y-4=0.$$ Chord $$BC:~M_{BC}(5,4),~m_{BC}=\frac{0-8}{6-4}=-4\Rightarrow m_\perp=\frac{1}{4}.$$ ⇒ $$y-4=\frac{1}{4}(x-5)\Rightarrow x-4y+11=0.$$ Solve: $$x+y-4=0,~x-4y+11=0\Rightarrow y=3,~x=1.$$ So centre $$(1,3).$$ Radius squared $$r^2=(1+4)^2+(3-0)^2=25+9=34.$$ Hence circle $$\boxed{(x-1)^2+(y-3)^2=34.}$$

Chapter 6 - Circles.question_text: The points $$A(-7,7),\ B(1,9),\ C(3,1),\ D(-7,1)$$ lie on a circle. (a) Find the perpendicular bisector of (i) $$AB$$ (ii) $$CD$$. (b) Hence find the equation of the circle.
Chapter 6 - Circles.hint: Use midpoint–slope for each chord: midpoint $$M=\big(\tfrac{x_1+x_2}{2},\tfrac{y_1+y_2}{2}\big)$$, slope $$m=\tfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$$, bisector slope $$m_\perp=-\tfrac1m$$ (vertical if segment is horizontal). Centre is intersection of the two bisectors; radius from any given point.
Chapter 6 - Circles.correct_answer: (a)(i) $$M_{AB}=\Big(\tfrac{-7+1}{2},\tfrac{7+9}{2}\Big)=(-3,8),\ m_{AB}=\tfrac{9-7}{1-(-7)}=\tfrac14\Rightarrow m_\perp=-4.$$ Line through $$(-3,8):\ y-8=-4(x+3)\Rightarrow \boxed{\,4x+y+4=0\,}.$$ (ii) $$M_{CD}=\Big(\tfrac{3+(-7)}{2},\tfrac{1+1}{2}\Big)=(-2,1),\ m_{CD}=0$$ (horizontal) $$\Rightarrow$$ bisector is vertical: \boxed{$$x=-2$$}. (b) Centre $$O$$ at the intersection: from $$x=-2$$ in $$4x+y+4=0\Rightarrow y=4$$, so $$O(-2,4).$$ Radius squared from $$A$$: $$r^2=(\!-2+7)^2+(4-7)^2=5^2+(-3)^2=34.$$ Hence the circle is \boxed{$$(x+2)^2+(y-4)^2=34$$}.
